The Story of Nagadatt Muni

I pay homage to the supreme fivefold guru, sovereigns of the realm of liberation, and write here the story of Nagadatt Muni.

In Rajgriha, capital of Magadh, there ruled King Prajapal — learned, generous, a devotee of the Jina. His queen Priyadharma bore two sons, Priyadharm and Priyamitra, both brilliant and upright. In time the brothers renounced the world, became Jain monks, and at the end of their lives performed the meditative death called samadhi-maran. They were reborn as gods in Achyut heaven.

The Heavenly Pact

There in heaven they made a solemn pact: "Whichever of us is reborn first as a human being, the other — still dwelling in heaven — shall descend to awaken him, stir his detachment, and inspire him to take Jain initiation for the sake of liberation." Having pledged this, they dwelt in bliss.

Priyadharm's heavenly lifespan ended first. He descended into the womb of Nagadatta, the beautiful queen of King Nagdharm of Ujjaini, and was born as Prince Nagadatt. From childhood, the boy showed a remarkable gift — he could play with snakes fearlessly, charming even the most venomous serpents. All who watched were astonished.

The Snake Charmer

One day Priyamitra, still a god in heaven, saw that the time had come to fulfil their pact. He assumed the disguise of a snake charmer and descended to Ujjaini. Carrying two fearsome serpents, he roamed the city performing for crowds and declaring that he would challenge any snake-handler who dared face him.

Word reached Nagadatt, who was already proud of his skill. He summoned the charmer at once. Arriving before the prince, Priyadharm said carefully, "I do not wish to perform tricks with royal princes where life is at risk. If I release my serpents before you and something goes wrong, what will the king do to me?" Nagadatt, brimming with confidence, insisted and even obtained his father's assurance of safety for the charmer.

Priyadharm first released a common snake. Nagadatt handled it easily, rendering it harmless within moments. His pride swelled. "Is this all you have? Bring out something worthy — a truly venomous serpent!"

The charmer warned him earnestly: "The second snake I carry is deadly beyond remedy. If it bites, there is no cure. Death is certain. Please, do not insist." But Nagadatt would not listen. "I have defeated thousands of serpents. What can this wretched creature do to me?"

Left with no choice, Priyadharm released the deadly serpent. It struck Nagadatt instantly. The prince collapsed, his body convulsing, his vision darkening. The court erupted in panic. Only then, hovering between life and death, did Nagadatt understand the folly of his pride.

By the grace of his past merit and the charmer's secret knowledge, the venom was drawn out and Nagadatt survived. But the experience shattered his attachment to the world. He had stared death in the face and seen how fragile life truly is.

Renunciation

Without lingering another moment, Nagadatt renounced his palace, his family, and his pride. He went into the forest, found the great monk Yamdhar, and took Jain initiation. Priyadharm then shed his disguise, revealed the whole story, paid his respects, and returned to heaven — his mission fulfilled.

As a monk, Nagadatt practiced fierce austerities. Day by day he purified his conduct until he became a jina-kalpi — a monk who wanders alone, in the manner of the Jina himself.

The Thieves and the Mother

One day, while on pilgrimage, Nagadatt passed through a fearsome forest that was a den of thieves. The bandits seized him, fearing he would reveal their hideout. Their leader Surdatt took one look at the serene monk and ordered his release. "This man is gentle and detached. You have done wrong to trouble him."

Soon after, Nagadatt's mother Nagadatta was travelling through the same forest with her daughter and valuables for a dowry. She encountered her son on the road and asked, "Master, is the way ahead safe?" The monk, maintaining perfect equanimity — for friend and foe were alike to him — gave no answer and walked on in silence.

The thieves then captured Nagadatta, stripped her of all her wealth, and took her daughter. When Surdatt learned what had happened, he was moved. "Look at that monk's detachment! His own mother bowed to him, yet he showed no partiality. We tormented him, yet he bore no hatred. Such are the truly great."

When Nagadatta learned the monk was her own son, she trembled with grief. "If only he had warned me! What use is a son who shows such cruelty?" She begged Surdatt for his knife, wishing to end her suffering.

Surdatt was deeply moved. "The mother of such a monk is my mother too. Forgive me!" He returned all her belongings and went to Nagadatt Muni, praised his virtues, and took initiation at his feet.

The Teaching

Surdatt, through austerity and right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct, destroyed his destructive karmas, attained omniscience, guided countless souls to welfare, and ultimately achieved the imperishable state of liberation. To have faith in the nature of the soul is right faith; to know it is right knowledge; to remain steadfast in it is right conduct. These three jewels together form the path to liberation. May Nagadatt and Surdatt Muni, who are like moons to the lotus-eyes of worldly beings, grant us peace.
